source: It was during the more pleasant weather, that in due rotation with the other seamen my first mast-head came round.

In most American whalemen the mast-heads are manned almost simultaneously with the vessel’s leaving her port; even though she may have fifteen thousand miles, and more, to sail ere reaching her proper cruising ground. And if, after a three, four, or five years’ voyage she is drawing nigh home with anything empty in her—say, an empty vial even—then, her mast-heads are kept manned to the last; and not till her skysail-poles sail in among the spires of the port, does she altogether relinquish the hope of capturing one whale more.

Now, as the business of standing mast-heads, ashore or afloat, is a very ancient and interesting one, let us in some measure expatiate here. I take it, that the earliest standers of mast-heads were the old Egyptians; because, in all my researches, I find none prior to them. For though their progenitors, the builders of Babel, must doubtless, by their tower, have intended to rear the loftiest mast-head in all Asia, or Africa either; yet (ere the final truck was put to it) as that great stone mast of theirs may be said to have gone by the board, in the dread gale of God’s wrath; therefore, we cannot give these Babel builders priority over the Egyptians. And that the Egyptians were a nation of mast-head standers, is an assertion based upon the general belief among archæologists, that the first pyramids were founded for astronomical purposes: a theory singularly supported by the peculiar stair-like formation of all four sides of those edifices; whereby, with prodigious long upliftings of their legs, those old astronomers were wont to mount to the apex, and sing out for new stars; even as the look-outs of a modern ship sing out for a sail, or a whale just bearing in sight. In Saint Stylites, the famous Christian hermit of old times, who built him a lofty stone pillar in the desert and spent the whole latter portion of his life on its summit, hoisting his food from the ground with a tackle; in him we have a remarkable instance of a dauntless stander-of-mast-heads; who was not to be driven from his place by fogs or frosts, rain, hail, or sleet; but valiantly facing everything out to the last, literally died at his post. Of modern standers-of-mast-heads we have but a lifeless set; mere stone, iron, and bronze men; who, though well capable of facing out a stiff gale, are still entirely incompetent to the business of singing out upon discovering any strange sight. There is Napoleon; who, upon the top of the column of Vendome, stands with arms folded, some one hundred and fifty feet in the air; careless, now, who rules the decks below; whether Louis Philippe, Louis Blanc, or Louis the Devil. Great Washington, too, stands high aloft on his towering main-mast in Baltimore, and like one of Hercules’ pillars, his column marks that point of human grandeur beyond which few mortals will go. Admiral Nelson, also, on a capstan of gun-metal, stands his mast-head in Trafalgar Square; and ever when most obscured by that London smoke, token is yet given that a hidden hero is there; for where there is smoke, must be fire. But neither great Washington, nor Napoleon, nor Nelson, will answer a single hail from below, however madly invoked to befriend by their counsels the distracted decks upon which they gaze; however it may be surmised, that their spirits penetrate through the thick haze of the future, and descry what shoals and what rocks must be shunned.

It may seem unwarrantable to couple in any respect the mast-head standers of the land with those of the sea; but that in truth it is not so, is plainly evinced by an item for which Obed Macy, the sole historian of Nantucket, stands accountable. The worthy Obed tells us, that in the early times of the whale fishery, ere ships were regularly launched in pursuit of the game, the people of that island erected lofty spars along the sea-coast, to which the look-outs ascended by means of nailed cleats, something as fowls go upstairs in a hen-house. A few years ago this same plan was adopted by the Bay whalemen of New Zealand, who, upon descrying the game, gave notice to the ready-manned boats nigh the beach. But this custom has now become obsolete; turn we then to the one proper mast-head, that of a whale-ship at sea. The three mast-heads are kept manned from sun-rise to sun-set; the seamen taking their regular turns (as at the helm), and relieving each other every two hours. In the serene weather of the tropics it is exceedingly pleasant the mast-head; nay, to a dreamy meditative man it is delightful. There you stand, a hundred feet above the silent decks, striding along the deep, as if the masts were gigantic stilts, while beneath you and between your legs, as it were, swim the hugest monsters of the sea, even as ships once sailed between the boots of the famous Colossus at old Rhodes. There you stand, lost in the infinite series of the sea, with nothing ruffled but the waves. The tranced ship indolently rolls; the drowsy trade winds blow; everything resolves you into languor. For the most part, in this tropic whaling life, a sublime uneventfulness invests you; you hear no news; read no gazettes; extras with startling accounts of commonplaces never delude you into unnecessary excitements; you hear of no domestic afflictions; bankrupt securities; fall of stocks; are never troubled with the thought of what you shall have for dinner—for all your meals for three years and more are snugly stowed in casks, and your bill of fare is immutable.

In one of those southern whalesmen, on a long three or four years’ voyage, as often happens, the sum of the various hours you spend at the mast-head would amount to several entire months. And it is much to be deplored that the place to which you devote so considerable a portion of the whole term of your natural life, should be so sadly destitute of anything approaching to a cosy inhabitiveness, or adapted to breed a comfortable localness of feeling, such as pertains to a bed, a hammock, a hearse, a sentry box, a pulpit, a coach, or any other of those small and snug contrivances in which men temporarily isolate themselves. Your most usual point of perch is the head of the t’ gallant-mast, where you stand upon two thin parallel sticks (almost peculiar to whalemen) called the t’ gallant cross-trees. Here, tossed about by the sea, the beginner feels about as cosy as he would standing on a bull’s horns. To be sure, in cold weather you may carry your house aloft with you, in the shape of a watch-coat; but properly speaking the thickest watch-coat is no more of a house than the unclad body; for as the soul is glued inside of its fleshy tabernacle, and cannot freely move about in it, nor even move out of it, without running great risk of perishing (like an ignorant pilgrim crossing the snowy Alps in winter); so a watch-coat is not so much of a house as it is a mere envelope, or additional skin encasing you. You cannot put a shelf or chest of drawers in your body, and no more can you make a convenient closet of your watch-coat.

Concerning all this, it is much to be deplored that the mast-heads of a southern whale ship are unprovided with those enviable little tents or pulpits, called crow’s-nests, in which the look-outs of a Greenland whaler are protected from the inclement weather of the frozen seas. In the fireside narrative of Captain Sleet, entitled “A Voyage among the Icebergs, in quest of the Greenland Whale, and incidentally for the re-discovery of the Lost Icelandic Colonies of Old Greenland;” in this admirable volume, all standers of mast-heads are furnished with a charmingly circumstantial account of the then recently invented crow’s-nest of the Glacier, which was the name of Captain Sleet’s good craft. He called it the Sleet’s crow’s-nest, in honor of himself; he being the original inventor and patentee, and free from all ridiculous false delicacy, and holding that if we call our own children after our own names (we fathers being the original inventors and patentees), so likewise should we denominate after ourselves any other apparatus we may beget. In shape, the Sleet’s crow’s-nest is something like a large tierce or pipe; it is open above, however, where it is furnished with a movable side-screen to keep to windward of your head in a hard gale. Being fixed on the summit of the mast, you ascend into it through a little trap-hatch in the bottom. On the after side, or side next the stern of the ship, is a comfortable seat, with a locker underneath for umbrellas, comforters, and coats. In front is a leather rack, in which to keep your speaking trumpet, pipe, telescope, and other nautical conveniences. When Captain Sleet in person stood his mast-head in this crow’s-nest of his, he tells us that he always had a rifle with him (also fixed in the rack), together with a powder flask and shot, for the purpose of popping off the stray narwhales, or vagrant sea unicorns infesting those waters; for you cannot successfully shoot at them from the deck owing to the resistance of the water, but to shoot down upon them is a very different thing. Now, it was plainly a labor of love for Captain Sleet to describe, as he does, all the little detailed conveniences of his crow’s-nest; but though he so enlarges upon many of these, and though he treats us to a very scientific account of his experiments in this crow’s-nest, with a small compass he kept there for the purpose of counteracting the errors resulting from what is called the “local attraction” of all binnacle magnets; an error ascribable to the horizontal vicinity of the iron in the ship’s planks, and in the Glacier’s case, perhaps, to there having been so many broken-down blacksmiths among her crew; I say, that though the Captain is very discreet and scientific here, yet, for all his learned “binnacle deviations,” “azimuth compass observations,” and “approximate errors,” he knows very well, Captain Sleet, that he was not so much immersed in those profound magnetic meditations, as to fail being attracted occasionally towards that well replenished little case-bottle, so nicely tucked in on one side of his crow’s nest, within easy reach of his hand. Though, upon the whole, I greatly admire and even love the brave, the honest, and learned Captain; yet I take it very ill of him that he should so utterly ignore that case-bottle, seeing what a faithful friend and comforter it must have been, while with mittened fingers and hooded head he was studying the mathematics aloft there in that bird’s nest within three or four perches of the pole.

But if we Southern whale-fishers are not so snugly housed aloft as Captain Sleet and his Greenlandmen were; yet that disadvantage is greatly counter-balanced by the widely contrasting serenity of those seductive seas in which we South fishers mostly float. For one, I used to lounge up the rigging very leisurely, resting in the top to have a chat with Queequeg, or any one else off duty whom I might find there; then ascending a little way further, and throwing a lazy leg over the top-sail yard, take a preliminary view of the watery pastures, and so at last mount to my ultimate destination.

Let me make a clean breast of it here, and frankly admit that I kept but sorry guard. With the problem of the universe revolving in me, how could I—being left completely to myself at such a thought-engendering altitude—how could I but lightly hold my obligations to observe all whale-ships’ standing orders, “Keep your weather eye open, and sing out every time.”

And let me in this place movingly admonish you, ye ship-owners of Nantucket! Beware of enlisting in your vigilant fisheries any lad with lean brow and hollow eye; given to unseasonable meditativeness; and who offers to ship with the Phædon instead of Bowditch in his head. Beware of such an one, I say; your whales must be seen before they can be killed; and this sunken-eyed young Platonist will tow you ten wakes round the world, and never make you one pint of sperm the richer. Nor are these monitions at all unneeded. For nowadays, the whale-fishery furnishes an asylum for many romantic, melancholy, and absent-minded young men, disgusted with the carking cares of earth, and seeking sentiment in tar and blubber. Childe Harold not unfrequently perches himself upon the mast-head of some luckless disappointed whale-ship, and in moody phrase ejaculates:—
“Roll on, thou deep and dark blue ocean, roll! Ten thousand blubber-hunters sweep over thee in vain.”

Very often do the captains of such ships take those absent-minded young philosophers to task, upbraiding them with not feeling sufficient “interest” in the voyage; half-hinting that they are so hopelessly lost to all honorable ambition, as that in their secret souls they would rather not see whales than otherwise. But all in vain; those young Platonists have a notion that their vision is imperfect; they are short-sighted; what use, then, to strain the visual nerve? They have left their opera-glasses at home.

“Why, thou monkey,” said a harpooneer to one of these lads, “we’ve been cruising now hard upon three years, and thou hast not raised a whale yet. Whales are scarce as hen’s teeth whenever thou art up here.” Perhaps they were; or perhaps there might have been shoals of them in the far horizon; but lulled into such an opium-like listlessness of vacant, unconscious reverie is this absent-minded youth by the blending cadence of waves with thoughts, that at last he loses his identity; takes the mystic ocean at his feet for the visible image of that deep, blue, bottomless soul, pervading mankind and nature; and every strange, half-seen, gliding, beautiful thing that eludes him; every dimly-discovered, uprising fin of some undiscernible form, seems to him the embodiment of those elusive thoughts that only people the soul by continually flitting through it. In this enchanted mood, thy spirit ebbs away to whence it came; becomes diffused through time and space; like Cranmer’s sprinkled Pantheistic ashes, forming at last a part of every shore the round globe over.

There is no life in thee, now, except that rocking life imparted by a gently rolling ship; by her, borrowed from the sea; by the sea, from the inscrutable tides of God. But while this sleep, this dream is on ye, move your foot or hand an inch; slip your hold at all; and your identity comes back in horror. Over Descartian vortices you hover. And perhaps, at mid-day, in the fairest weather, with one half-throttled shriek you drop through that transparent air into the summer sea, no more to rise for ever. Heed it well, ye Pantheists!

But neither great Washington, nor Napoleon, nor Nelson will answer a single hail from below, however madly they are invoked to help with their counsel the distracted decks they gaze down on — however it may be surmised that their spirits penetrate the thick haze of the future and see what shoals and what rocks must be avoided.

It may seem unjustified to link the masthead-standers of the land with those of the sea in any way, but that in truth it is not is plainly shown by a detail for which Obed Macy, the sole historian of Nantucket, is our source. Worthy Obed tells us that in the early days of the whale fishery, before ships were regularly sent out in pursuit, the islanders erected tall poles along the coast, to which lookouts climbed by means of nailed rungs, like chickens going up stairs in a henhouse. A few years ago, the same system was adopted by the bay whalemen of New Zealand, who, upon spotting whales, signaled the waiting boats near the beach. But this custom is now obsolete. So let us turn to the proper masthead: that of a whale ship at sea. The three mastheads are manned from sunrise to sunset, the sailors taking regular turns (as at the helm) and relieving each other every two hours. In the calm weather of the tropics, the masthead is exceedingly pleasant; no, to a dreamy, meditative man it is delightful. There you stand, a hundred feet above the silent decks, striding across the deep as if the masts were giant stilts. Beneath you and between your legs, so to speak, swim the largest monsters of the sea, just as ships once sailed between the boots of the famous Colossus of Rhodes. There you stand, lost in the infinite series of the sea, with nothing stirred but the waves. The hypnotized ship lazily rolls. The drowsy trade winds blow. Everything dissolves you into lethargy. For the most part, in this tropical whaling life, a sublime uneventfulness wraps around you. You hear no news. You read no newspapers. No extras with alarming reports of ordinary events trick you into unnecessary excitement. You hear of no family troubles or bankrupt investments or falling stocks. You never worry about what to have for dinner — all your meals for three years or more are snugly stowed in casks, and your menu is fixed.

On one of those southern whalers, on a long voyage of three or four years, as often happens, the hours you spend at the masthead add up to several whole months. And it's a great pity that the place where you spend so large a share of your entire natural life should be so sadly lacking in anything like cozy homeliness, or anything suited to breeding a comfortable sense of belonging to a spot, such as goes with a bed, a hammock, a hearse, a sentry box, a pulpit, a coach, or any of those other small, snug contraptions in which men shut themselves away for a time. Your usual perch is the top of the topgallant mast, where you stand on two thin parallel sticks (almost unique to whalemen) called the topgallant crosstrees. Up there, tossed about by the sea, the beginner feels roughly as cozy as he would standing on a bull's horns. Of course, in cold weather you can take your house aloft with you in the form of a watch-coat; but strictly speaking, the thickest watch-coat is no more a house than your bare body is. For just as the soul is glued inside its fleshly tabernacle, and can't move around freely in it, or even move out of it, without great risk of perishing (like an ignorant pilgrim crossing the snowy Alps in winter), so a watch-coat is not so much a house as a mere envelope, or an extra skin wrapped around you. You can't put a shelf or a chest of drawers inside your body, and neither can you make a handy closet out of your watch-coat.

On all this, it is much to be regretted that the mastheads of a southern whale ship are not provided with those enviable little tents or pulpits called crow's-nests, in which the lookouts of a Greenland whaler are protected from the inclement weather of the frozen seas. In the fireside narrative of Captain Sleet, titled "A Voyage among the Icebergs, in quest of the Greenland Whale, and incidentally for the re-discovery of the Lost Icelandic Colonies of Old Greenland" — in this admirable volume, all masthead-standers are furnished with a charmingly circumstantial account of the then recently invented crow's-nest of the Glacier, which was the name of Captain Sleet's good ship. He called it the Sleet's crow's-nest, in honor of himself, since he was the original inventor and patentee, and free from all ridiculous false delicacy; and he held that if we name our own children after ourselves (we fathers being the original inventors and patentees), we should likewise name after ourselves any other apparatus we may beget. In shape, the Sleet's crow's-nest is something like a large tierce or pipe (both big casks); it is open above, however, where it is fitted with a movable side-screen to keep to windward of your head in a hard gale. Since it is fixed on the top of the mast, you climb into it through a little trap-hatch in the bottom. On the after side, the side nearest the stern of the ship, is a comfortable seat, with a locker underneath for umbrellas, comforters, and coats. In front is a leather rack in which to keep your speaking trumpet, pipe, telescope, and other nautical conveniences. When Captain Sleet in person stood his masthead in this crow's-nest of his, he tells us that he always had a rifle with him (also fixed in the rack), together with a powder flask and shot, for the purpose of popping off the stray narwhales, or vagrant sea unicorns, infesting those waters; for you cannot shoot at them successfully from the deck, owing to the resistance of the water, but to shoot down on them is a very different thing. Now, it was plainly a labor of love for Captain Sleet to describe, as he does, all the little detailed conveniences of his crow's-nest. But though he enlarges on many of these, and though he treats us to a very scientific account of his experiments in this crow's-nest with a small compass he kept there to counteract the errors resulting from what is called the "local attraction" of all binnacle magnets — an error attributable to the horizontal nearness of the iron in the ship's planks, and, in the Glacier's case, perhaps to there having been so many broken-down blacksmiths among her crew — I say, though the Captain is very discreet and scientific here, yet for all his learned "binnacle deviations," "azimuth compass observations," and "approximate errors," he knows very well, Captain Sleet, that he was not so immersed in those profound magnetic meditations as not to be attracted now and then toward that well-replenished little case-bottle so nicely tucked in on one side of his crow's-nest, within easy reach of his hand. Though, on the whole, I greatly admire and even love the brave, the honest, and learned Captain, yet I take it very ill of him that he should so utterly ignore that case-bottle, seeing what a faithful friend and comforter it must have been while, with mittened fingers and hooded head, he was studying the mathematics up there in that bird's nest within three or four perches of the pole.

But if we southern whale-fishers aren't as snugly housed aloft as Captain Sleet and his Greenlandmen were, that disadvantage is greatly offset by the sharply contrasting serenity of those seductive seas where we mostly sail. For one, I used to lounge up the rigging quite leisurely, resting in the top for a chat with Queequeg or anyone else off duty I might find there. Then I'd climb a little higher, throw a lazy leg over the topsail yard, take a preliminary survey of the watery pastures, and at last reach my final destination.

Let me make a clean confession here and frankly admit that I kept a poor watch. With the problem of the universe revolving in my head, how could I — left completely alone at such a thought-provoking altitude — how could I take seriously my duty to observe all whale-ship standing orders: "Keep your weather eye open and sing out every time."

And let me here movingly warn you ship-owners of Nantucket! Beware of enlisting in your vigilant fisheries any lad with a lean brow and hollow eye, given to unseasonable meditation, who offers to ship with the Phaedon (Plato's dialogue on the immortality of the soul) instead of Bowditch (the standard navigation manual) in his head. Beware of such a one, I say: your whales must be seen before they can be killed, and this sunken-eyed young Platonist will tow you ten wakes around the world and never make you one pint of sperm the richer. Nor are these warnings at all unneeded. For nowadays the whale fishery provides an asylum for many romantic, melancholy, and absent-minded young men, disgusted with the gnawing cares of earth, and seeking sentiment in tar and blubber. Childe Harold not infrequently perches himself on the masthead of some luckless, disappointed whale ship, and in moody phrases exclaims:
"Roll on, thou deep and dark blue ocean, roll! Ten thousand blubber-hunters sweep over thee in vain."

Very often the captains of such ships scold these absent-minded young philosophers, criticizing them for not taking enough "interest" in the voyage — half-hinting that they are so hopelessly lost to all honorable ambition that they would secretly rather not see whales at all. But it's useless. These young Platonists have a theory that their vision is imperfect. They are nearsighted. What use, then, to strain their eyes? They've left their opera glasses at home.

"Why, you monkey," said a harpooner to one of these lads, "we've been cruising now hard on three years, and you haven't spotted a whale yet. Whales are as scarce as hen's teeth whenever you're up here." Perhaps they were. Or perhaps there might have been whole schools of them on the far horizon. But lulled into such an opium-like daze of vacant, unconscious daydreaming is this absent-minded youth — by the blending rhythm of waves and thoughts — that at last he loses his identity. He takes the mystic ocean at his feet for the visible image of that deep, blue, bottomless soul pervading all mankind and nature. Every strange, half-glimpsed, gliding, beautiful thing that escapes him, every dimly perceived rising fin of some unidentifiable form, seems to him the embodiment of those elusive thoughts that populate the soul by continually flitting through it. In this enchanted state, your spirit ebbs away to where it came from, becoming diffused through time and space, like Cranmer's sprinkled Pantheistic ashes, forming at last a part of every shore the round globe over.

There is no life in you now, except the rocking life given by a gently rolling ship — borrowed from the sea, and by the sea from the unfathomable tides of God. But while this sleep, this dream is upon you, move your foot or hand an inch — slip your grip even slightly — and your identity comes rushing back in horror. Over Descartian vortices you hover. And perhaps, at midday, in the fairest weather, with one half-strangled shriek you drop through that transparent air into the summer sea, never to rise again. Take heed, you Pantheists!

modern_da.title: Kapitel 35 — Mastetoppen
paragraphs: Det var i det behageligere vejr, at min første tur i mastetoppen kom, i rigtig rækkefølge med de andre sømænd.

På de fleste amerikanske hvalfangere bliver mastetoppene bemandet næsten, så snart skibet forlader havnen, selv om hun måske har femten tusind engelske mil eller mere at sejle, før hun når sit rette fangstområde. Og hvis hun efter en rejse på tre, fire eller fem år er på vej hjem med noget, der ikke er fyldt — selv bare en tom flaske — så forbliver hendes mastetoppe bemandet til det sidste. Først når hendes skysejlsstænger, de allerøverste ender af masterne, sejler ind mellem havnebyens spir, opgiver hun håbet om at få endnu en hval.

Nu er det at stå i mastetoppen, på land som til søs, en meget gammel og interessant beskæftigelse, så lad os gå lidt mere i dybden med den her. Jeg regner med, at de allerførste mastetopsstandere var de gamle ægyptere, for i al min læsning finder jeg ingen før dem. For selv om deres forfædre, Babels bygmestre, sikkert har ment, at deres tårn skulle være den højeste mastetop i hele Asien, eller Afrika for den sags skyld, så kan man dog, eftersom deres store stenmast (før den sidste knop, træhætten allerøverst på en mast, nåede at blive sat på) kan siges at være gået over bord i Guds frygtelige vredesstorm, ikke give disse Babels bygmestre forrang for ægypterne. Og at ægypterne var et folk af mastetopsstandere er en påstand, der bygger på arkæologernes almindelige opfattelse, at de første pyramider blev grundlagt til astronomiske formål — en teori, der på en enestående måde understøttes af den ejendommelige trappelignende form på alle fire sider af disse bygninger, som disse gamle astronomer med enormt lange løft af benene plejede at klatre op ad til toppen og råbe ud om nye stjerner, ligesom udkigsmændene på et moderne skib råber ud om et sejl eller en hval, der lige er kommet til syne. I Sankt Stylites, den berømte kristne eneboer i gamle dage, som byggede sig en høj stensøjle i ørkenen og tilbragte hele den sidste del af sit liv på toppen af den, hvor han hejste sin mad op fra jorden med en talje — i ham har vi et bemærkelsesværdigt eksempel på en uforfærdet mastetopsstander, som ikke lod sig drive fra sin plads af tåge eller frost, regn, hagl eller slud, men som tappert trodsede alt til det sidste og bogstaveligt talt døde på sin post. Af moderne mastetopsstandere har vi kun en livløs flok: blot mænd af sten, jern og bronze, som godt nok kan holde stand mod en hård storm, men alligevel er fuldstændig udygtige til at råbe ud, når de opdager noget mærkeligt. Der er Napoleon, som står med korslagte arme oven på Vendôme-søjlen, omkring hundrede og halvtreds fod oppe i luften, ligeglad nu med, hvem der hersker på dækkene dernede, om det er Louis Philippe, Louis Blanc eller Louis Djævelen. Den store Washington står også højt oppe på sin tårnhøje hovedmast i Baltimore, og ligesom en af Herkules' søjler markerer hans søjle det punkt af menneskelig storhed, som få dødelige vil nå ud over. Admiral Nelson står også sin mastetop på et gangspil af kanonmetal på Trafalgar Square; og selv når han er mest skjult af den londonske røg, er der stadig et tegn på, at en skjult helt er der; for hvor der er røg, må der være ild. Men hverken den store Washington eller Napoleon eller Nelson vil svare på et eneste anråb nedefra, uanset hvor vildt de bliver påkaldt for at hjælpe med deres råd de fortumlede dæk, de ser ned på — selv om man kan formode, at deres ånder trænger igennem fremtidens tykke tåge og ser, hvilke grunde og hvilke klipper der må undgås.

Det kan synes uberettiget på nogen måde at sammenkæde landets mastetopsstandere med havets, men at det i sandhed ikke er det, fremgår tydeligt af en enkelt detalje, som Obed Macy, Nantuckets eneste historiker, er vores kilde til. Den hæderlige Obed fortæller os, at øboerne i hvalfangstens første tid, før skibe jævnligt blev sendt ud efter dem, rejste høje stænger langs kysten, hvor udkigsmænd klatrede op ad påsømmede trin, som høns, der går op ad trappen i et hønsehus. For nogle år siden blev det samme system taget i brug af bugtfangerne i New Zealand, der, når de havde set hvaler, gav tegn til de ventende både nær stranden. Men denne skik er nu forladt. Lad os derfor gå til den egentlige mastetop: den på et hvalfangerskib til søs. De tre mastetoppe er bemandet fra solopgang til solnedgang, og sømændene tager faste ture (som ved roret) og afløser hinanden hver anden time. I det stille vejr i troperne er mastetoppen overordentlig behagelig; nej, for en drømmende, grublende mand er den henrivende. Dér står du, hundrede fod over de tavse dæk, og skrider hen over dybet, som var masterne kæmpestylter. Under dig og, så at sige, mellem dine ben svømmer havets største uhyrer, ligesom skibe en gang sejlede mellem støvlerne på den berømte Rhodos-kolos. Dér står du, fortabt i havets uendelige række, hvor intet røres undtagen bølgerne. Det hypnotiserede skib vugger dovent. De søvnige passatvinde blæser. Alt opløser dig i sløvhed. For det meste hviler der i dette tropiske hvalfangerliv en ophøjet begivenhedsløshed omkring dig. Du hører ingen nyheder. Du læser ingen aviser. Ingen ekstraudgaver med alarmerende beretninger om hverdagsbegivenheder narrer dig ind i unødig ophidselse. Du hører ikke om familietrængsler eller konkursramte investeringer eller faldende aktier. Du bekymrer dig aldrig om, hvad du skal have til middag — alle dine måltider i tre år eller mere ligger lunt stuvet væk i tønder, og din menu er fast.

På en af de sydlige hvalfangere, på en lang rejse på tre eller fire år, som det ofte sker, løber de timer, du tilbringer i mastetoppen, op til flere hele måneder. Og det er rigtig ærgerligt, at det sted, hvor du tilbringer så stor en del af hele dit naturlige liv, skal være så ynkeligt blottet for noget, der ligner hyggelig hjemlighed, eller noget, der kan skabe en behagelig følelse af at høre til på et sted, sådan som der følger med en seng, en hængekøje, en ligvogn, et skilderhus, en prædikestol, en karet eller nogen af de andre små, lune indretninger, som mennesker lukker sig inde i for en tid. Din sædvanlige siddeplads er toppen af bramstangen, hvor du står på to tynde parallelle stokke (næsten enestående for hvalfangere) kaldet bramsalingerne. Deroppe, kastet rundt af havet, føler en nybegynder sig omtrent lige så hjemmevant, som hvis han stod på en tyrs horn. Selvfølgelig kan du i koldt vejr tage dit hus med dig op i form af en vagtfrakke; men strengt taget er den tykkeste vagtfrakke ikke mere et hus, end din nøgne krop er. For ligesom sjælen er limet fast inde i sit kødelige tabernakel og ikke kan bevæge sig frit rundt i det, eller endda flytte ud af det, uden stor fare for at gå til grunde (som en uvidende pilgrim, der krydser de snedækkede Alper om vinteren), således er en vagtfrakke ikke så meget et hus som blot en omhyllende konvolut eller en ekstra hud viklet om dig. Du kan ikke sætte en hylde eller en kommode ind i din krop, og du kan heller ikke lave et praktisk skab ud af din vagtfrakke.

Med hensyn til alt dette er det meget at beklage, at mastetoppene på et sydligt hvalfangerskib ikke er forsynet med de misundelsesværdige små telte eller prædikestole, der kaldes tønder i masten, hvor udkigsmændene på en grønlandsfanger beskyttes mod det barske vejr i de frosne have. I kaptajn Sleets fortælling ved kaminen, med titlen »En rejse blandt isbjergene på jagt efter den grønlandske hval og tillige for at genopdage de tabte islandske kolonier i det gamle Grønland« — i dette beundringsværdige bind får alle mastetopsstandere en henrivende udførlig beretning om den dengang nyligt opfundne tønde i masten på Glacier, som var navnet på kaptajn Sleets gode skib. Han kaldte den Sleets tønde i masten til ære for sig selv, da han var den oprindelige opfinder og patenthaver og fri for al latterlig falsk finfølelse; og han mente, at hvis vi opkalder vores egne børn efter os selv (vi fædre er jo de oprindelige opfindere og patenthavere), så skal vi også opkalde alle andre apparater, vi skaber, efter os selv. I form ligner Sleets tønde i masten noget en stor tierce eller pibe (begge store tønder); den er dog åben foroven, hvor den er forsynet med en bevægelig sideskærm, der holder sig til luvart for dit hoved i en hård storm. Da den er fastgjort øverst på masten, kravler du ind i den gennem en lille faldlem i bunden. På bagsiden, den side der er nærmest skibets agterende, er et behageligt sæde med et skab under til paraplyer, halstørklæder og frakker. Foran er et læderstativ, hvor du kan opbevare dit talerør, din pibe, din kikkert og andre søfartsbekvemmeligheder. Når kaptajn Sleet selv stod i mastetoppen i denne sin tønde, fortæller han os, at han altid havde en riffel med (også fastgjort i stativet) sammen med en krudtflaske og kugler for at kunne skyde de omstrejfende narhvaler, eller vagabonderende havenhjørninger, der hjemsøgte disse farvande; for du kan ikke skyde på dem med held fra dækket på grund af vandets modstand, men at skyde ned på dem er en helt anden sag. Nu var det tydeligvis en kærlighedsgerning for kaptajn Sleet at beskrive, som han gør, alle de små udførlige bekvemmeligheder i sin tønde. Men selv om han bredder sig om mange af dem, og selv om han forkæler os med en meget videnskabelig beretning om sine eksperimenter i denne tønde med et lille kompas, han havde der for at modvirke de fejl, der skyldes den såkaldte »lokale tiltrækning« på alle kompashusets magneter — en fejl, der skyldes jernets vandrette nærhed i skibets planker og i Glaciers tilfælde måske også at der var så mange udslidte smede blandt hendes besætning — jeg siger, selv om kaptajnen her er meget diskret og videnskabelig, og trods alle hans lærde »kompashusafvigelser«, »azimutkompasobservationer« og »tilnærmede fejl«, ved han udmærket, kaptajn Sleet, at han ikke var så fordybet i de dybsindige magnetiske betragtninger, at han ikke nu og da følte sig draget mod den velfyldte lille kasseflaske, der så pænt var puttet ind på den ene side af hans tønde, inden for let rækkevidde af hans hånd. Selv om jeg i det hele taget højt beundrer og endda elsker den modige, ærlige og lærde kaptajn, tager jeg det ham dog meget ilde op, at han så fuldstændig ignorerer den kasseflaske, når man tænker på, hvilken trofast ven og trøster den må have været, mens han med luffer på fingrene og hætte på hovedet studerede matematik deroppe i det fuglerede inden for tre eller fire stænger fra polen.

Men selv om vi hvalfangere fra de sydlige have ikke sidder lige så lunt deroppe som kaptajn Sleet og hans grønlandsfarere, bliver den ulempe rigeligt opvejet af den modsatte ro i de lokkende farvande, hvor vi mest sejler. Jeg for min part plejede at slentre op i rigningen i fuld ro og mag og hvile i mærsen for at sludre med Queequeg eller en anden, der havde fri og skete at være der. Så klatrede jeg lidt højere, svang et dovent ben over mærsrå, tog en indledende rundtur over de vandige græsgange og nåede til sidst mit endelige mål.

Lad mig nu aflægge en ren tilståelse og åbent indrømme, at jeg holdt en elendig udkigsvagt. Med universets gåde snurrende rundt i hovedet — hvordan skulle jeg, helt alene i en højde, der så kraftigt får en til at tænke, kunne tage min pligt alvorligt, nemlig at følge alle hvalfangerskibets faste ordrer: »Hold øjnene åbne og råb op hver eneste gang.«

Og lad mig her gribende advare jer skibsredere i Nantucket! Pas på at hyre nogen dreng med smal pande og hule øjne, der er tilbøjelig til meditation på forkerte tidspunkter, og som melder sig til hyre med Phaedon (Platons dialog om sjælens udødelighed) i hovedet i stedet for Bowditch (den almindelige lærebog i navigation). Pas på sådan en, siger jeg: jeres hvaler skal ses, før de kan dræbes, og denne huløjede unge platoniker vil slæbe jer ti kølvande rundt om jorden, uden at han nogensinde gør jer en eneste pot spermolie rigere. Disse advarsler er heller ikke overflødige. I vore dage er hvalfangsten nemlig et asyl for mange romantiske, tungsindige og adspredte unge mænd, der er trætte af jordens nagende bekymringer og søger følelse i tjære og spæk. Childe Harold sætter sig ikke sjældent op på mastetoppen af et uheldigt, skuffet hvalfangerskib og udbryder i mørke vendinger:
»Rul på, du dybe, mørkeblå ocean, rul! Ti tusind spækjægere sejler hen over dig forgæves.«

Meget ofte skælder kaptajnerne på sådanne skibe ud på disse adspredte unge filosoffer og bebrejder dem, at de ikke viser nok »interesse« for rejsen — de antyder halvt, at de er så håbløst fortabt for al hæderlig ærgerrighed, at de i det skjulte helst slet ikke ville se hvaler. Men det nytter ikke. Disse unge platonikere har en teori om, at deres syn er ufuldkomment. De er nærsynede. Hvad nytter det så at anstrenge øjnene? De har glemt deres teaterkikkert derhjemme.

»Hør her, din abekat,« sagde en harpuner til en af disse drenge, »vi har nu krydset rundt i næsten tre år, og du har ikke set en eneste hval endnu. Hvaler er lige så sjældne som hønsetænder, hver gang du er deroppe.« Det var de måske. Eller måske var der hele stimer af dem ved den fjerne horisont. Men denne adspredte dreng er så indlullet i en opiumsagtig døs af tomme, ubevidste dagdrømme — af bølgernes og tankernes sammensmeltende rytme — at han til sidst mister sig selv. Han tager det mystiske hav for sine fødder for det synlige billede af den dybe, blå, bundløse sjæl, der gennemtrænger hele menneskeheden og naturen. Hvert eneste mærkelige, halvt skimtede, glidende, smukke væsen, der slipper væk fra ham, hver svagt anede finne på en eller anden uidentificerbar skikkelse, forekommer ham at være selve legemliggørelsen af de flygtige tanker, der befolker sjælen ved uafbrudt at flagre gennem den. I denne fortryllede tilstand ebber din ånd ud mod det sted, hvor den kom fra, og spredes ud over tid og rum, som Cranmers udstrøede, panteistiske aske, indtil den til sidst bliver en del af hver kyst på den runde klode.

Der er intet liv i dig nu, bortset fra det vuggende liv, som et blidt rullende skib giver dig — lånt fra havet og af havet fra Guds ufattelige tidevand. Men mens denne søvn, denne drøm hviler over dig, så flyt blot en tomme på fod eller hånd — lad blot grebet glide lidt — og din identitet vender tilbage med et rædselsfuldt ryk. Over descartesiske hvirvler svæver du. Og måske styrter du ved middagstid, i det smukkeste vejr, med ét halvkvalt skrig gennem den gennemsigtige luft ned i sommerhavet og kommer aldrig op igen. Pas på, I panteister!
